title: Reflection: how mirrors send light back

summary.text: This unit is about reflection. Reflection is light bouncing off something. A mirror is a very smooth, shiny surface that sends light back in neat order, so you see a picture in it. The light bounces off a mirror at the same slant it came in, like a ball off a wall. A mirror turns things round from front to back, so writing looks backwards in it. Mirror writing is writing done backwards on purpose, so it reads properly in a mirror. Deep down, the tiny electrons in a mirror's metal catch light and send it back out. Mirrors help us cook, drive safely, look at stars and even measure the distance to the Moon. Some questions are still open, like why so few animals know their own face in a mirror.
summary.art: A child holding a hand mirror that bounces a bright spot of sunlight onto a wall, while backwards writing on a card reads properly in the mirror.

intro.hook: Pick up a steel spoon. Look at your face in the inside of the bowl. Now turn the spoon over and look at the back. What happened to your face?
intro.text: On the inside of the spoon, your face is upside down. On the back, it is the right way up, but tiny with a big nose. The spoon has no light of its own. So where is your face coming from? It is your own light, sent back to you. This unit is about how shiny things send light back. Scientists call it reflection.
intro.art: A child's surprised face shown twice: upside down in the hollow of a steel spoon, and right way up and small on the back of the spoon.

outcomes: I can say what reflection is: light bouncing off something.
I can show with a torch and a mirror that light bounces off a mirror at the same slant it came in.
I can explain why a mirror shows a picture but a white wall does not.
I can read and write mirror writing, and say why a mirror makes writing look backwards.
I can count the pictures made by two mirrors, and find shapes that look the same in a mirror.
I can give examples of how people use mirrors, from car mirrors to telescopes and Moon lasers.
I can say what scientists agree about mirrors, and what is still open, like why only some animals know their own reflection.

terms.meaning: What lets us see. It comes from light sources like the Sun, a bulb or a flame.
terms.example: In a room with no light at all, you cannot see your own hand.
terms.art: A sunbeam coming through a window onto a floor.

terms.meaning: Light bouncing off something. Every thing you see is sending some light back to your eyes.
terms.example: Your face in a mirror is light bouncing off you, then off the mirror, into your eyes.
terms.art: A light ray arrow hitting a mirror and bouncing off at the same slant.

terms.meaning: To bounce light back. A mirror reflects light very well.
terms.example: A steel plate reflects the light of the kitchen bulb.
terms.art: A shiny steel thali with the bulb's bright spot in it.

terms.meaning: A very smooth, shiny surface that reflects light in neat order. That is why you see a picture in it.
terms.example: The bathroom mirror, a car's side mirror and a still pond are all mirrors.
terms.art: A round hand mirror showing a child's smiling face.

terms.meaning: The picture you see in a mirror. It looks like a real thing behind the glass, but nothing is there.
terms.example: Your image in the mirror seems to stand behind the wall.
terms.art: A child at a mirror, with a faint dotted copy of the child standing behind the glass.

terms.meaning: Something that makes its own light.
terms.example: The Sun and a diya are light sources. A mirror is not. It only bounces light.
terms.art: A lit diya beside a mirror in a dark room, the mirror shining only where the diya's light hits it.

terms.meaning: A thin, straight line of light. We draw it as a line with an arrow.
terms.example: A sunbeam through a gap in the curtains is a bundle of rays.
terms.art: A narrow beam of sunlight crossing a dusty room.

terms.meaning: How tilted a line is. Scientists call it the angle.
terms.example: Light that hits a mirror at a steep slant leaves at the same steep slant.
terms.art: Two arrows meeting a mirror like a V, both at the same tilt.

terms.meaning: Writing done backwards, from right to left with every letter turned round. It reads properly in a mirror.
terms.example: The word AMBULANCE is written backwards on the front of an ambulance.
terms.art: The word AMBULANCE written backwards on an ambulance's bonnet, reading properly in a car's rear-view mirror.

terms.meaning: When one half of a shape is the mirror picture of the other half.
terms.example: A butterfly, a leaf and the letter A are symmetrical.
terms.art: A butterfly with a dotted line down its middle.

terms.meaning: The fold line that splits a shape into two mirror halves.
terms.example: Fold a heart shape down the middle. Both halves match exactly.
terms.art: A paper heart folded down its middle line.

terms.meaning: A tiny bit inside every atom. In metals, some electrons can move about freely.
terms.example: The thin silver or aluminium behind mirror glass is full of free electrons. They catch light and send it back.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle on a mirror showing tiny dots jiggling and sending out wiggly light.

terms.meaning: A tube with mirrors inside. The mirrors make many copies of a few beads, in a pattern.
terms.example: Turn a kaleidoscope and the bead flower changes shape.
terms.art: The view inside a kaleidoscope: a six-sided flower of coloured beads.

terms.meaning: Something made to send light straight back to where it came from.
terms.example: Bicycle reflectors and the cat's eyes in the middle of a highway shine in car headlights.
terms.art: A red bicycle reflector glowing in a car's headlight beam at night.

explanations.definition: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface and travelling away again.
explanations.description: Light travels out from a light source, like the Sun or a bulb. When it hits something, some of it bounces off. That bounce is reflection. Almost everything reflects some light. That is how you see a book, a cup or a friend. A mirror is special. It reflects nearly all the light, and it keeps the light in neat order.
examples: A steel tumbler in the sun throws a bright spot on the wall.
A still pond shows the trees upside down above it.
The Moon makes no light. It shines because it reflects sunlight.
explanations.art: A bulb sending rays out to a book, a cup and a mirror, with each one bouncing some rays back.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what reflection is.

explanations.concept: Light bounces at the same slant
explanations.definition: When light hits a mirror, it leaves at the same slant that it came in. Scientists say the angle in equals the angle out.
explanations.description: Throw a ball at a wall at a slant. It bounces away at the same slant on the other side. Light does the same thing off a mirror. Shine a torch straight at a mirror, and the light comes straight back. Shine it in from the left at a slant, and it leaves to the right at the same slant. This rule lets you aim light, like aiming a ball.
examples: Shine a torch at a mirror from the left. The bright spot lands on the right.
Stand straight in front of a mirror and you see your own eyes. Stand to one side and you see the far side of the room.
Carrom players use the same rule. The striker bounces off the edge at the same slant it hit.
explanations.art: A torch beam hitting a mirror and bouncing off like a V, with two equal angles marked by curved arcs.
explanations.context: This card explains the rule for how light bounces off a mirror. You test it in the Catch the Bouncing Beam experiment.

explanations.concept: Why a mirror shows a picture and a wall does not
explanations.definition: A smooth surface sends all the light back in the same neat order. A rough surface scatters the light every which way.
explanations.description: A white wall reflects a lot of light. So why can't you see your face in it? Zoom in, and the wall is bumpy, like a ploughed field. Each bump sends light off in a different direction. The light gets mixed up, so there is no picture. A mirror is so smooth that every bit of light bounces the same way. The light stays in order, so your eyes see a clear picture.
examples: A new steel plate shows your face. A scratched old one only shows a blur.
Calm water shows the trees clearly. When the wind makes ripples, the picture breaks up.
Polished marble floors in a temple show the lamps. A rough stone floor does not.
explanations.art: Two zoomed-in surfaces side by side: a flat mirror with rays bouncing back in neat parallel lines, and bumpy paper with rays scattering every way.
explanations.context: This card explains why a mirror shows a picture of you, but a white wall does not, even though both reflect light.

explanations.concept: Where the mirror picture seems to be
explanations.definition: Your image seems to stand behind the mirror, exactly as far behind it as you are in front of it.
explanations.description: Look into a mirror and the room seems to carry on behind the glass. Nothing is really there. The light bounces off the mirror and into your eyes. Your eyes and brain think light travels in straight lines. So they guess the light came from behind the glass. Step back one step, and your image steps back one step too. Your image is also the same size as you.
examples: Stand one big step from a mirror. Your image looks two big steps away from you.
A small mirror can still show a whole big room behind you.
Shops put mirrors on one wall so the shop looks twice as big.
explanations.art: A child one step in front of a mirror, and a dotted mirror-child one step behind the glass, with footprints marking equal distances.
explanations.context: This card explains where the picture in a mirror seems to be, and why it is not really there.

explanations.concept: Does a mirror swap left and right?
explanations.description: Raise your right hand in front of a mirror. The mirror person raises the hand on the same side as yours. Yet we say they raised their left hand. So what does a mirror really swap? Scientists agree on what the light does. People still argue about why it feels like left and right.
examples: Your watch on your left wrist appears on the mirror person's right wrist.
A mirror does not turn you upside down, even though it could seem to.
Writing held up to a mirror reads from right to left.

perspectives.explanation: A mirror does not swap left and right at all. It swaps front and back. Your nose points at the mirror, and the image's nose points back at you. Left stays on the left side, and up stays up.

perspectives.who: Ned Block, an American philosopher, in 1974
perspectives.explanation: It feels like left and right swap because we imagine walking round behind the glass to stand where the image is. When we turn round, our own left and right change places. If we imagined flipping head over heels instead, we would say mirrors swap up and down.

perspectives.who: Richard Gregory, a British scientist who studied seeing, in his 1997 book Mirrors in Mind
perspectives.explanation: Most of the puzzle is about how we turn things round in our minds. A book held up to the mirror is turned round by our own hands before the mirror ever sees it. That turning is where left and right seem to swap.

explanations.art: A child raising one hand at a mirror, with arrows showing the hand and its image on the same side, and a nose-to-back arrow showing what is flipped.
explanations.context: This card is about a famous puzzle: does a mirror really swap left and right? There are different explanations.

explanations.definition: Mirror writing is writing that runs backwards, from right to left, with every letter turned round. Held up to a mirror, it reads normally.
explanations.description: A mirror turns things round from front to back. So writing seen in a mirror runs backwards. If you write backwards on purpose, the mirror turns it round the right way again. That is why ambulances have their name written backwards on the front. A driver in front sees it in the rear-view mirror and reads AMBULANCE. Writing seen through the back of a window, or through thin paper, also looks like mirror writing.
examples: The great Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci, about 500 years ago, filled his notebooks with mirror writing. He was left-handed.
In the 1871 book Through the Looking-Glass, Alice finds a poem printed backwards. She holds it up to a mirror to read it.
Many young children write some letters backwards, like b and d, while they are learning. This is very common and normal.
explanations.art: A page of mirror writing next to a hand mirror, with the words reading correctly in the mirror.
explanations.context: This card explains mirror writing: writing done backwards so it reads properly in a mirror.

explanations.definition: Most mirrors are a sheet of glass with a very thin layer of shiny metal, like silver or aluminium, on the back.
explanations.description: The first mirrors were still water. About 8,000 years ago, people in Anatolia, in today's Turkey, polished a black volcanic glass called obsidian into mirrors. Later people polished bronze and copper. In Kerala, craftspeople in Aranmula still make mirrors of polished metal by hand, called Aranmula kannadi. In 1835 a German chemist, Justus von Liebig, found a way to coat glass with a thin layer of silver. That made bright mirrors cheap. Today most mirrors use aluminium.
examples: A still bucket of water is a mirror.
A polished steel tumbler or thali is a mirror made of metal.
An Aranmula kannadi from Kerala is a metal mirror with no glass at all.
explanations.art: A row of mirrors through time: a pond, an obsidian disc, a bronze hand mirror, an Aranmula kannadi and a modern glass mirror.
explanations.context: This card explains what mirrors are made of, from ponds long ago to the glass mirror in your bathroom.

explanations.concept: Deep down: electrons send the light back
explanations.definition: In a metal, free electrons are shaken by the light that hits them. As they shake, they send out new light, which is the reflected light.
explanations.description: Zoom into the thin metal layer of a mirror. It is made of atoms. Some of their electrons are free to move about. Light is a quick wobble of electric and magnetic push. When light hits the metal, it shakes those free electrons. Shaking electrons send out light of their own. That new light goes back out from the mirror. So a reflection is not light that never touched anything. It is light passed on by trillions of tiny electrons.
examples: Metals are shiny because they have free electrons. Wood and cloth do not, so they are not shiny.
Silver reflects about 95 out of every 100 parts of the light that hits it.
The force that makes a mirror shine is the same electric force that makes friction and holds atoms together.
explanations.art: A huge zoom into a mirror's silver layer: wobbly light arriving, tiny electrons jiggling, and new wobbly light leaving.
explanations.context: This card zooms right in to the atoms in a mirror, to see what reflection really is.

explanations.definition: When two mirrors face each other, light can bounce from one to the other again and again. Each bounce makes another picture.
explanations.description: Stand two mirrors like an open book. Put a toy between them. Light from the toy bounces once to make some pictures. It bounces twice, three times and more to make others. The smaller the gap between the mirrors, the more pictures you see. With two mirrors facing each other, the pictures seem to go on for ever. But each bounce loses a little light. So the far pictures get darker and a little greenish, and then fade away.
examples: Two mirrors at a right angle, like the corner of a book, make 3 pictures of a toy.
A kaleidoscope uses three mirrors to turn a few beads into a whole flower.
In a lift or a salon with mirrors on facing walls, you see a long tunnel of yourself.
explanations.art: A toy elephant between two mirrors standing like an open book, with five copies of the elephant arranged in a circle.
explanations.context: This card explains why two mirrors make many pictures of one thing.

explanations.definition: Some animals have mirrors built into their bodies. They are made of tiny stacked crystals or layers that reflect light.
explanations.description: A cat's eyes shine in torchlight. A layer at the back of each eye works like a mirror. It sends light back through the eye a second time, so the cat sees better in dim light. Many silvery fish have mirror scales. A scallop, a kind of shellfish, has up to 200 tiny eyes. Each eye uses a curved mirror made of square crystals, found in 2017. A deep-sea spookfish uses mirrors in its eyes too.
examples: Cows, dogs and cats have eyes that shine in headlights. Human eyes do not.
Silvery fish like the sardine are hard to see in water, because their sides reflect the water around them.
Shiny beetles and peacock feathers reflect light from thin layers, not from paint.
explanations.art: A cat's eyes glowing in torchlight beside a scallop with a row of tiny blue eyes along its shell.
explanations.context: This card is about animals that carry real mirrors in their bodies. These animals do not make light. They reflect it.

explanations.concept: Do animals know their own reflection?
explanations.description: When you look in a mirror, you know the face is you. Most animals do not seem to. They bark at it, or try to play with it. Scientists test this with a mark. They put a small dot on an animal where it can only see it in a mirror. If the animal touches the dot on its own body, it seems to know that the image is itself.
examples: Babies start to pass the mark test at about 18 months old.
Chimpanzees passed it in 1970, in tests by the American scientist Gordon Gallup.
An elephant in a zoo passed it in 2006, and magpies, a kind of bird, in 2008.

perspectives.explanation: Touching the dot shows the animal has an idea of itself. Only a few kinds of animals pass, such as great apes, elephants, dolphins and magpies.

perspectives.who: Masanori Kohda and his team in Japan, in 2019
perspectives.explanation: A tiny fish called the cleaner wrasse also scraped at a mark it could only see in a mirror. So either small fish know themselves, or the test does not measure what we think.
The test favours animals that use their eyes most. A dog knows the world by smell, so a mirror may just not interest it. Failing the test does not prove an animal has no sense of self.

explanations.art: A chimpanzee touching a coloured dot on its own forehead while looking in a mirror.
explanations.context: This card is about the mirror test, which asks whether an animal knows the face in the mirror is its own. Scientists disagree about what it shows.

explanations.concept: Is nature the same in a mirror?
explanations.description: Your two hands are mirror pictures of each other. Many tiny molecules come in two mirror forms too, like a left and a right glove. Living things almost always use only one of the two forms. Nobody knows for sure why. Some scientists think it happened by chance when life began. Others think something in nature tipped the balance.
examples: In 1848 the French scientist Louis Pasteur found that some crystals come in left-handed and right-handed forms.
The building blocks of the proteins in your body are nearly all the left-handed kind.
In 1957 the Chinese-American scientist Chien-Shiung Wu showed that one of nature's forces, the weak force, does not act the same in a mirror world.
explanations.art: A left glove and a right glove facing each other across a mirror, with two tiny ball-and-stick molecules doing the same.
explanations.context: This card goes far out from mirrors, to a big open question: would the world work just the same if it were flipped like a mirror?

explanations.concept: Mirrors that look at the sky
explanations.definition: Big telescopes use curved mirrors to collect faint light from stars and bring it together into a picture.
explanations.description: A curved mirror can gather lots of light into one small spot. In 1668 Isaac Newton built a telescope with a mirror instead of a glass lens. Today the biggest telescopes all use mirrors. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, has 18 six-sided mirrors coated in a thin layer of gold. Together they are 6.5 metres wide. In India, at Devasthal near Nainital, a telescope uses a spinning pool of liquid metal as its mirror.
examples: A torch has a curved mirror behind the bulb to send its light forward.
Astronauts on Apollo 11 left a set of mirrors on the Moon in 1969. Scientists still bounce laser light off them.
Rows of mirrors can bounce sunlight onto one spot to make heat for cooking.
explanations.art: The gold honeycomb mirror of the James Webb Space Telescope floating in space with a starry background.
explanations.context: This card follows mirrors out to space: how giant mirrors help us see faraway stars.

agreed.text: Light bounces off a flat mirror at the same slant that it came in.
agreed.evidence: Hero of Alexandria wrote about mirrors about 2,000 years ago. Ibn al-Haytham tested it carefully about 1,000 years ago, in his Book of Optics. Children test it with a torch and a mirror every day.

agreed.text: A smooth, shiny surface shows a clear picture. A rough surface scatters the light, so it shows no picture.
agreed.evidence: Ripples on a pond break up the picture of the trees. When the water goes still, the picture comes back.

agreed.text: A flat mirror's image is the same size as the thing, and as far behind the mirror as the thing is in front.
agreed.evidence: You can measure it. Put a candle in front of a sheet of glass. Its image lines up with a second candle placed the same distance behind.

agreed.text: Mirrors reflect because of free electrons in their metal layer.
agreed.evidence: Metals, which have free electrons, are shiny. Wood, cloth and stone are not. Scientists can predict how shiny a metal will be from its electrons.

agreed.text: No mirror reflects all the light. A little is always lost.
agreed.evidence: In two mirrors facing each other, the far pictures get darker. Even the best mirrors scientists make lose a tiny bit at every bounce.

challenging.claim: A mirror shows you exactly as you are.
challenging.who: A common belief. People say 'the mirror never lies'.
challenging.for: A flat mirror shows your real size and shape, with every hair in place.
challenging.against: A mirror shows you turned round, front to back. Your friends see you the other way round. A curved mirror at a mela stretches you tall or squashes you short. And a mirror loses a little light, so you look a tiny bit darker.
challenging.context: This card is about the saying that a mirror shows us exactly as we are.

challenging.claim: Archimedes set Roman ships on fire with mirrors.
challenging.who: A story told about the Greek thinker Archimedes, written down hundreds of years after he lived
challenging.for: Mirrors really can focus sunlight to make fire. In 2005, students at a university in America lit a still wooden model of a ship using 127 mirrors.
challenging.against: No writer from his own time tells the story. Real ships move, and on a cloudy day it would fail. Most historians think it is a legend.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous old story of mirrors used as a weapon. Is it true?

challenging.claim: A mirror swaps left and right.
challenging.for: Writing looks backwards, and a right hand seems to become a left hand.
challenging.against: A mirror really swaps front and back. Your raised hand stays on the same side. The left-right feeling comes from imagining turning round.
challenging.context: This card is about the common saying that mirrors swap left and right.

challenging.claim: Writing backwards means a child is doing something wrong.
challenging.who: An old way of thinking in many schools
challenging.for: Backwards letters are harder for others to read.
challenging.against: Many children reverse letters while learning. Most grow out of it by about age 7. Leonardo da Vinci wrote backwards all his life and was one of the greatest thinkers ever. Mirror writing is a real skill.
challenging.context: This card is about how people used to think about children who write backwards.

challenging.claim: Our brains have special mirror cells that copy what others do.
challenging.who: Giacomo Rizzolatti and his team in Parma, Italy, who studied monkeys in the 1990s
challenging.for: Some brain cells in monkeys fired both when a monkey grabbed food and when it watched someone else grab food.
challenging.against: In 2014 the scientist Gregory Hickok wrote a book called The Myth of Mirror Neurons. He and others say these cells do not explain how we understand each other.
challenging.context: This card is about a new and argued-about idea: that our brains mirror other people.

big_questions.q: Is the face in the mirror really you?
big_questions.hint: It moves when you move. But it is made of light that bounced. Is a photo of you, you?

big_questions.q: You have never seen your own face directly. How do you know what you look like?
big_questions.hint: Think of mirrors, photos, water and what other people tell you.

big_questions.q: If you put two perfect mirrors face to face, would the pictures go on for ever?
big_questions.hint: Each bounce loses a little light. Can anything in the world be perfect?

big_questions.q: Why can you see yourself in a steel plate but not in a wooden one?
big_questions.hint: Zoom in. What does steel have that wood does not?

big_questions.q: Could you build a mirror that reflects every bit of light?
big_questions.hint: The best mirrors scientists make lose less than one part in ten thousand. Is zero possible?

big_questions.q: Why does almost all of life use only one of the two mirror forms of some molecules?
big_questions.hint: Nobody knows. Was it luck, or did something tip the balance?

big_questions.q: When we say someone is 'reflecting', we mean they are thinking about themselves. Why do you think we use the same word as for mirrors?
big_questions.hint: What comes back to you when you think about what you did today?

big_questions.q: Is it fair that some children were scolded for writing backwards?
big_questions.hint: Leonardo da Vinci wrote backwards. Is different the same as wrong?

big_questions.q: Indra's net is an old picture of jewels that each reflect all the others. Are people a bit like that?
big_questions.hint: Think of how you smile when someone smiles at you.

story.title: Written for the Mirror
story.note: Imagined. Noor, Jiba, Kanji, Bhimji and the chai stall are made up. Kutch mirror-work embroidery is real. Ambulances in India really do have their name written backwards on the front. Leonardo da Vinci, who is not in the story, really did write his notebooks in mirror writing.
text: Noor's left hand had its own ideas. When she wrote slowly, her letters faced the way Miss Thakkar's letters faced on the blackboard. When she wrote fast, they ran the other way. They started at the right edge of the page and marched to the left. Every letter was turned round, like a fish flipped over in a pan.
"Again, Noor," Miss Thakkar would sigh. She was not unkind, only tired. "The other way." And somebody at the back would whisper "Ulta Noor", upside-down Noor, and the whole row would giggle.

Noor lived in a village on the dry, flat land near Bhuj, in Kutch. In the afternoons the wind came off the Rann, the great salt desert, and threw dust at everything. Her grandmother Jiba sat in the doorway of their mud house, because that was where the light was best. Jiba did mirror-work. She stitched tiny round mirrors, no bigger than a fingernail, onto cloth. Each mirror sat inside a little ring of red and yellow thread.
"Each one holds a piece of the sky," Jiba liked to say. When she tilted the cloth, a hundred bright spots danced across the floor.

One day Noor came home and threw her notebook onto the floor. Jiba did not scold her. She picked up the book and looked at the page. A whole line ran backwards, from right to left. Then Jiba took one loose mirror from her tin. She stood it on its edge, at the end of the line.
"Look," she said.
Noor bent down. In the tiny circle of glass, her backward words had turned round. They read the right way, as neat as print. MY NAME IS NOOR.
"Your hand is not wrong," said Jiba. "It writes for the mirror."
Noor stared. She turned the notebook over and held the page up to the sunlit door. From the back, through the thin paper, her words also read the right way round.

That month, Noor's uncle Kanji opened a chai stall on the road to Bhuj. Trucks passed it all day, carrying salt from the Rann. The stall had a real glass window, and Kanji was very proud of it. He paid Bhimji, the sign painter, to paint CHAI KANJI on it in fat red letters.
"Paint it on the inside," said Kanji. "Then the dust storms can't scrub it off."
Bhimji stood inside the stall and painted beautiful letters, curly and red. He stepped back, pleased. Then he went outside to look.
A truck had stopped. The driver was leaning out of his window and laughing. From the road, the sign read backwards. Every letter was flipped, from right to left, like Noor's fast writing.

Bhimji scratched his head. He tried again with the letters turned the other way. But his hand had painted the right way round for thirty years. It would not turn. His second sign was a muddle, half one way and half the other. He wiped it off, and he left for a wedding job in Anjar, two hours away. The big mela started the next day. Hundreds of trucks would pass. Kanji sat on his bench with his head in his hands.

Noor stood on the road and looked at the clean glass. Then she went inside and looked out through it. The trucks went by. The world through the glass was the same. But anything painted on this side would be seen from the other side. It would be seen from the back, the way she had seen her notebook against the sunny door.
From the back, words turn round. So the road could only read the right way what was painted backwards on the inside.
"I can do it," said Noor.
Kanji looked at her. Then he looked at the empty glass, and at the road. He handed her the brush.

Noor did not think about each letter. Thinking made her hand slow, and slow was the wrong way. She let her left hand run, fast, the way it always wanted to. The red letters marched from right to left across the glass. Inside the stall, they looked like nonsense.
She put down the brush and walked out onto the road.
CHAI KANJI, said the window, the right way round, in fat red letters. A truck slowed down. The driver read the sign, smiled and pulled over for tea.

Later that afternoon, a white ambulance went past, with its siren wailing. Noor saw the word on its bonnet and read it at once, without any mirror. AMBULANCE was written backwards, right to left, every letter flipped.
"Why is it written like that?" asked a boy at the stall.
"So the driver in front can read it in his mirror," said Kanji. "In the mirror it turns round."
Noor said nothing. But she smiled, because it was written in her writing.

Jiba walked down to the stall at sunset with a strip of cloth over her arm. It was covered in tiny mirrors. She tied it along the top of the window. When the low sun hit it, each little mirror threw a bright spot across the dusty road, a row of small suns, there and gone as the cloth moved.

The next morning, in class, Noor wrote slowly, the way Miss Thakkar wrote on the board. At the very bottom of her page, she added one more line. She wrote it fast, from right to left, every letter turned round. It was for anyone who had a mirror.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a mirror turns things round from front to back. So does looking at something from behind, like writing seen through the back of a window or a thin page. Noor's fast writing was already the mirror's way round. The sign painter's skill was the wrong one for painting on the inside of the glass, and Noor's 'mistake' was exactly right. Mirror writing is not broken writing. It is writing made for the other side. The ambulance shows the same idea in real life. The story also quietly asks whether different is the same as wrong.
ask: Why did the sign look backwards from the road when Bhimji painted it the normal way?
What did Jiba's little mirror do to Noor's backward writing?
Why is AMBULANCE written backwards on the front of an ambulance?
Why couldn't Bhimji just turn his letters round? What was easy for Noor that was hard for him?
Is there something you do differently from other people that might be just right somewhere?

games.title: Mirror or Not?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: 24 cards to cut out
items: TEST IT: hold the mirror under the word BOX. What happens?
TEST IT: write your name in mirror writing. Can the mirror read it?
TEST IT: draw half a heart. Can the mirror finish it?
TEST IT: look at the word ECNALUBMA in the mirror. What does it say?

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide: will this look the SAME when a mirror stands beside it, or will it CHANGE? Put the card on that mat.
Then test it with a mirror stood upright beside the card. If you were right, win one star.
If you draw a TEST IT card, everyone does the test together. The first person to explain what happened wins two stars.
When the cards run out, the player with the most stars wins.
games.context: Mirror or Not? is a card game about what a mirror does to letters and words. For each card, players guess whether it will look the same in a mirror stood beside it, then test it.

setup.art: Two paper mats on a table labelled SAME and CHANGES, a pile of face-down letter cards and a small hand mirror.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the SAME and CHANGES mats. Put the cards face down.

setup.art: A child holding a mirror upright beside a card with the word MOM, which looks exactly the same in the mirror.
setup.caption: 2. Guess, then test each card with the mirror.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the two mats. 2. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. 3. Put the mirror and the star tokens in the middle.
flow.say: Each card has a letter or a word. Guess: will it look the same in a mirror, or will it change? Then we test it.
flow.kid: Put out the two mats. Mix up the cards. For each card, guess: SAME or CHANGES in a mirror? Then test it!
flow.context: This is the first step of Mirror or Not?, a card game about what a mirror does to letters. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play the card 'A' together as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card: the letter A. Same or changes?
flow.kid: Practice card: the letter A. Same or changes? Tap, then test it.

check.q: Stand a mirror beside the letter A. What will you see?
options: An A that looks just the same
check.why: Game moment: the letter A has a line of symmetry straight down its middle. Its left half is the mirror picture of its right half. So the mirror shows the same A. Letters like B and R have no up-and-down line of symmetry, so they turn round.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, guesses, then tests with the mirror. 2. Give a star for each right guess.
flow.say: Say why you think it will stay the same or change, before you test.
flow.kid: Take turns. Guess SAME or CHANGES. Say why. Test it. A right guess wins a star.
flow.parent: Letters that stay the same in a mirror stood beside them: A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y. Words stay the same only if every letter is one of these, and the word reads the same backwards, like MOM, WOW, TOOT, OTTO and YAY. DAD and NOON change, because D and N turn round. The BOX card is a surprise: with the mirror under the word, B, O and X look the same upside down, so BOX stays BOX.

flow.do: When someone draws the NOON card, stop and talk about it.
flow.say: NOON reads the same backwards. So why does it change in the mirror?
flow.kid: NOON reads the same backwards. But look in the mirror. Why does it change?

check.q: NOON reads the same backwards. Why does it still look wrong in a mirror?
options: The letter N turns round in a mirror
The O turns into a zero
check.why: Game moment: a mirror does two things to a word. It reverses the order of the letters, and it turns each letter round. NOON survives the first, but each N turns round. Only words made of symmetrical letters, like MOM, survive both.

flow.do: Count the stars. The player with the most wins.
flow.say: Who has the most stars? What was the trickiest card?
flow.kid: Count your stars. Which card surprised you most?
flow.think: Can you invent a new word that looks the same in a mirror?

games.title: Bounce Relay
games.players: 3 or more players, best with a family or group of friends

printables.title: A target poster to stick on the wall
items: A big paper target with three rings: 1 point, 2 points, 3 points

printables.title: Bounce Relay score sheet
items: Did the light reach the target?

rules: Stick the target on a wall in a dim room. Put the torch on a pile of books, aimed away from the target.
Round 1: one player must bounce the torch beam onto the target with their mirror.
Round 2: two players. The light must bounce off both mirrors before it reaches the target.
Score the ring the light lands in. More bounces means harder, so double the points from round 3.
Never let the beam shine into anyone's eyes. If it does, that round scores zero.
games.context: Bounce Relay is a team game. Players hold mirrors and pass a torch beam from one mirror to the next until it lands on a target. It comes from the founder's idea of a relay where each step must bounce light with a mirror.

setup.art: A torch on a pile of books in a dim room, its beam hitting a mirror held by one child, then bouncing to a second child's mirror, then onto a paper target on the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Each player holds a mirror. Pass the beam along.

setup.art: A paper target with three rings on a wall, with a bright torch spot in the middle ring.
setup.caption: 2. Land the beam on the target to score.

flow.do: 1. Stick the target on a wall. 2. Put the torch on books so its beam points away from the target. 3. Dim the room.
flow.say: The torch is pointing the wrong way. We must use mirrors to send its light to the target.
flow.kid: The torch points away from the target. Use mirrors to send the light there!
flow.parent: Use plastic mirrors if you can. Remind everyone: the beam must never go into anyone's eyes.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bounce Relay, a team game where players pass a torch beam from mirror to mirror onto a target.

flow.do: Round 1: one player tilts their mirror to land the beam on the target.
flow.say: Where must you stand, and how must you tilt the mirror?
flow.kid: Round 1. Stand in the beam. Tilt your mirror. Land the light on the target!

check.q: The beam lands too far to the left of the target. What should you do?
options: Tilt the mirror a little, so the light leaves at a new slant
Hold the mirror further from the light
check.why: Game moment: the light leaves the mirror at the same slant it arrives. Tilt the mirror, and you change the slant, so the spot moves. Small tilts make big moves on a far wall.

flow.do: Rounds 2 and 3: add a second and a third mirror.
flow.say: Now the light must visit two mirrors. Who should stand where?
flow.kid: Round 2: two mirrors. Round 3: three mirrors. Plan where everyone stands first!
flow.parent: Players will find it easier to plan from the target backwards. Each mirror must face halfway between where the light comes from and where it must go.

flow.do: Add up the points and talk about the game.
flow.say: What made it hard with three mirrors? Did the spot get dimmer?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Was the spot dimmer after three mirrors? Why?

ask.q: Why was the spot dimmer after three bounces?
good: Each mirror keeps a little of the light.
The beam spreads out over a longer path.

items.p: What is reflection?
opts: Light being made by a mirror
The dark part behind a thing
items.why: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. Picking 'made by a mirror' usually means thinking a mirror is a light source. It only sends back light that reaches it. The dark part behind a thing is a shadow, which is a different idea.

items.p: Which of these is NOT a light source?
opts: A torch that is switched on
items.why: A mirror makes no light. In a dark cupboard it shows nothing at all. It only bounces light from somewhere else. Picking the torch usually means remembering that torches have shiny parts, but a switched-on torch makes its own light.

items.p: When light hits a mirror, it bounces off at the same ____ that it came in.
items.why: Light leaves a mirror at the same slant it arrived, on the other side, like a ball bouncing off a wall.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one show a clear picture of your face, or only shine?
items: a phone screen that is switched off
items.why: Smooth, shiny surfaces send light back in neat order, so they show a picture. Rough surfaces scatter light every way, so there is no picture.

items.p: A white wall reflects light.
items.why: True. A white wall reflects a lot of light. That is why a white room looks bright. But the wall is rough, so the light scatters and there is no picture.

items.p: Why can you see your face in a mirror but not in a white wall?
opts: The mirror is smooth, so it sends light back in neat order
The mirror is a light source
The wall is too far away
items.why: Both reflect light. But the wall's tiny bumps send light every which way, and the picture gets mixed up. Picking 'the mirror is a light source' is a common mix-up. Neither of them makes light.

items.p: Match each thing to what it does with light.
items.why: Only light sources make light. Everything else reflects some light, scatters it or soaks it up.

items.p: Stand one big step in front of a mirror. Where does your image seem to be?
opts: One big step behind the glass
On the surface of the glass
Two big steps behind the glass
items.why: Your image seems as far behind the mirror as you are in front. Picking 'on the surface' is a very common guess. But try touching your image: it always seems to be further away than the glass.

items.p: Writing that runs backwards, so it reads properly in a mirror, is called ____ writing.
items.why: Mirror writing runs from right to left, with each letter turned round. A mirror turns it the right way again.

items.p: Why is the word AMBULANCE written backwards on the front of an ambulance?
opts: So drivers in front can read it in their mirrors
So people behind can read it
items.why: A rear-view mirror turns writing round. So the word is painted backwards, and the mirror turns it the right way for the driver in front.

items.p: Put the steps of the bouncing-beam test in order.
items: Make a thin beam with a slit card on the torch
Stand the mirror on the top edge of the paper
Aim the beam at the middle of the mirror from the left
Mark where the bounced beam lands on the right
items.why: First you make the beam and set up the mirror. Then you aim and mark where the light goes.

items.p: A mirror makes things look upside down.
items.why: False. A flat mirror keeps up as up. Only a curved mirror, like the inside of a spoon, can flip a picture upside down.

items.p: Draw a torch, a flat mirror and an eye. Draw the path of the light from the torch to the mirror, then to the eye. Use a ruler.
items.a: Two straight lines with arrows. One goes from the torch to the mirror. The other goes from the mirror to the eye, at the same slant on the other side.
items.why: Light travels in straight lines and bounces off at the same slant it came in.
items.art: A blank page with a torch on the left, a mirror at the top and an eye on the right.

items.p: Which letter looks the SAME when you stand a mirror beside it?
items.why: The letter A has a line of symmetry straight down its middle, so its mirror picture is the same. B, R and F have no such line, so they turn round. Picking B often means noticing B's top and bottom match. That is a different line of symmetry, side to side.

items.p: Your little cousin says a mirror is a light source because it is so bright. What would you say? Use the word reflect.
items.a: A mirror is not a light source. It only reflects light from the Sun or a bulb. In a dark cupboard, a mirror shows nothing at all.
items.why: A light source makes its own light. A mirror only reflects light that reaches it.

items.p: Two mirrors standing like an open book make more than one picture of a toy.
items.why: True. Light bounces between the two mirrors, and each bounce makes another picture. At a quarter-circle gap you see 3 pictures.

items.p: A torch starts 8 cm to the left of the middle line and aims at the middle of the mirror. Where will the bounced beam reach the bottom edge?
opts: About 8 cm right of the middle line
About 8 cm left of the middle line
items.why: Light leaves at the same slant on the other side. So 8 cm left goes to about 8 cm right. Picking 16 cm often means adding the two sides together.

items.p: You shine a torch straight at a mirror, head on. Where does the light go?
items.why: Head on in means head on out. With no slant, the light comes straight back. Picking left or right usually means remembering the V shape, which only happens when light comes in at a slant.

items.p: To see your whole body in a mirror, you need a mirror at least as tall as you.
items.why: False. You only need a mirror half as tall as you, wherever you stand. Try it with sticky notes on a mirror.

items.p: Two mirrors at a quarter-circle gap make 3 pictures. At a sixth gap they make ____ pictures.
items.why: The number of slices that fit in a whole circle, take away 1. 6 slices take away 1 is 5.

items.p: In two mirrors facing each other, why do the far pictures fade?
opts: Each bounce loses a little light
The pictures move away too fast
items.why: No mirror sends back every bit of light. After many bounces, very little is left. Picking 'light slows down' is a common idea. Light does not slow down when it bounces, but some of it is kept by the mirror each time.

items.p: Match each old mirror to what it was made of.
pairs: glass with a thin metal layer
items.why: People have always looked for smooth, shiny surfaces. Water came first, then obsidian, then metals, then metal-backed glass.

items.p: Deep down, what sends light back from a mirror?
opts: Free electrons in its metal layer
items.why: Light shakes the free electrons in the thin metal layer, and they send the light back out. The glass is mostly there to keep the metal smooth and safe. Picking 'the glass' is very common, but clear glass on its own lets most light through.

items.p: Your friend raises her right hand. You are her mirror. Which hand do you raise, and why?
items.a: I raise my left hand. A mirror keeps everything on the same side of the room. My left hand is on the same side as her right hand, because we face each other.
items.why: A mirror swaps front and back, not left and right. Copying like a mirror means using the hand on the same side of the room.

items.p: The Sheesh Mahal at Amber Fort is covered in tiny mirrors. Why does a lamp make it sparkle so much?
opts: Each tiny mirror reflects the lamp's light to your eyes
The mirrors make their own light
items.why: Each mirror bounces light towards you from a slightly different place. So one lamp seems to become hundreds of sparkles.

items.p: Sort these animals. Which ones have mirror-like parts in their bodies?
items.why: Cats have a reflecting layer at the back of their eyes. Scallops have tiny mirror eyes. Silvery fish have mirror scales. Human eyes have no reflecting layer, which is why they do not shine in headlights.

items.p: A cat's eyes shine in the dark because they make their own light.
items.why: False. A cat's eyes reflect light, like a mirror. In total darkness they do not shine at all.

items.p: The scientist who invented the kaleidoscope in 1816 was David ____.
items.why: David Brewster was a Scottish scientist who studied light. He named the kaleidoscope from Greek words meaning 'looking at beautiful shapes'.

items.p: Draw two mirrors standing like an open book, with a toy between them. Draw all the pictures of the toy you would see at a quarter gap.
items.a: Two mirrors at a right angle, one real toy and 3 pictures of the toy, arranged in a ring.
items.why: At a quarter-circle gap, two mirrors make 3 pictures.

items.p: Which word looks the same when you stand a mirror beside it?
items.why: W and O are symmetrical down the middle, and WOW reads the same backwards. NOON, BOB and POP read the same backwards, but N, B and P turn round in a mirror.

items.p: Why do you think shops put a big mirror on one wall?
items.a: The mirror makes the shop look twice as big, because the room seems to carry on behind the glass. It also makes the shop look brighter.
items.why: Your image seems as far behind the mirror as the thing is in front. So the whole room seems to carry on behind the glass.

items.p: A mirror is said to swap left and right. Explain what it really swaps.
items.a: A mirror really swaps front and back. If I raise my right hand, the image raises the hand on the same side of the room. Its nose points back at me. It only feels like left and right because I imagine turning round to stand where the image is.
items.why: Physicists say mirrors swap front and back. The left-right feeling comes from imagining ourselves turned round.

items.p: You look at a word through two mirrors, one bounce after the other. How does it look?
items.why: Each mirror turns the word round once. Two turns put it back the right way. Picking 'backwards' is right for one mirror only.

items.p: Astronauts left mirrors on the Moon in 1969. What do scientists use them for?
opts: To measure how far away the Moon is, by bouncing laser light off them
items.why: Scientists send a laser pulse to the Moon and time how long the reflection takes to come back. That tells them the distance very exactly. It shows the Moon moves about 3.8 cm further from Earth every year.

items.p: The best mirrors scientists can make reflect every single bit of light.
items.why: False. Even the best mirrors lose a tiny part of the light at every bounce, less than one part in ten thousand. No mirror is perfect.

items.p: A tiny fish, the cleaner wrasse, scraped at a mark it could only see in a mirror. Why did this surprise scientists?
opts: They thought only big-brained animals could pass the mirror test
items.why: Before 2019, only apes, elephants, dolphins and a few birds had passed. The fish result made scientists argue about what the test really shows.

items.p: Leonardo da Vinci wrote his notebooks in mirror writing. Give two reasons he might have done it. Then say which you think is most likely.
items.a: He was left-handed, so writing right to left meant he did not smudge the ink. Or he wanted to keep his ideas a little secret. I think not smudging is most likely, because the ink was wet.
items.why: Nobody knows for sure. Not smudging the ink and privacy are the two most common ideas.

items.p: Why are metals shiny, but wood is not?
opts: Metals have free electrons that send light back
items.why: Free electrons in metals are shaken by light and send it straight back. Wood has no free electrons, and its surface is rough, so it scatters and soaks up the light.

items.p: Two mirrors are at an eighth-of-a-circle gap. How many pictures of a toy between them?
items.why: 8 slices fit in a whole circle. Take away 1 for the real toy's slice. 8 minus 1 is 7. Picking 8 means counting the real toy as a picture.

items.p: Match each use of mirrors to what it does.
pairs: A cat's eye on a highway
sends headlight beams back to the driver
Rows of curved mirrors at a solar kitchen
bounce sunlight onto one spot to make heat
items.why: All of them use the same rule: a mirror sends light off at the same slant it came in. Curved mirrors can bring lots of light together into one spot.

items.p: A mirror only half as tall as you can show your whole body.
items.why: True. Your image of your head uses a patch of mirror halfway between your eyes and the top of your head. The same for your feet. So you need half your height.

items.p: Your hands are mirror pictures of each other. Many tiny molecules in living things also come in two mirror forms. What is strange about which form life uses?
items.a: Life almost always uses only one of the two forms. For example, the building blocks of our proteins are nearly all the left-handed kind. Nobody knows for sure why.
items.why: This is an open question in science. Scientists have ideas, but nobody knows the answer yet.

items.p: Why do the far pictures in two facing mirrors look a little green?
opts: The glass soaks up a little more of the other colours
items.why: Ordinary mirror glass lets green light through a little more easily than other colours. After many trips through the glass, the light left over looks greenish.

items.p: Design a road sign that a driver can read in the rear-view mirror. Draw the sign as it must be painted.
items.a: The word or picture is painted backwards, from right to left, with every letter turned round.
items.why: The mirror turns the sign round, so it must be painted the mirror's way to read correctly.

items.p: Put these in order, from the oldest to the newest.
items: Hero of Alexandria writes about mirrors
items.why: About 8,000 years ago, about 2,000 years ago, about 1,000 years ago, 1668, 1835 and 2021.

items.p: Is the face in the mirror really you? Give a reason for your answer.
items.a: Any honest answer with a reason is good. For example: 'Yes, because it moves when I move.' Or: 'No, it is only light that bounced off me.'
items.why: This is a big question with no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason.

experiments.title: Catch the Bouncing Beam: does light bounce like a ball?
experiments.question: When a thin beam of light hits a mirror at a slant, where does it go?
experiments.predict: Before you switch on the torch, point to where you think the bounced beam will land. Will it come straight back, go to the same side, or go to the other side?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, always aim at the same spot on the mirror, the middle mark. Change only one thing: how far to the left the torch starts. Try each start point twice, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a torch
a small flat mirror, plastic if you have one
a ball of plasticine or two books, to stand the mirror up
a piece of card with a thin slit cut in it, or a comb
a large sheet of paper, a pencil and a ruler
tape

experiments.safety: Never shine the torch into anyone's eyes, either straight or bounced off the mirror. A grown-up cuts the slit in the card. If the mirror is glass, hold it by its edges and keep it in its frame.

schedule.what: Make a thin beam. Aim it at the mirror from 3 start points. Mark where it lands. Draw the lines and fold the paper.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw each beam with a ruler: one line in to the mirror, one line out. Fold the paper along the middle line and see if the lines match.
experiments.context: This is the bouncing-beam experiment. You shine a thin beam of torchlight at a mirror from the side, and mark where it bounces to.

setup.art: A torch lying on a table with a piece of card taped over its glass, the card having one thin slit, making a thin line of light on the paper.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a card with a thin slit over the torch. Now it makes a thin beam.

setup.art: A small mirror standing upright on the top edge of a big sheet of paper, with a pencil line running straight down from the middle of the mirror to the bottom edge.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the mirror on the top edge of the paper. Draw a middle line straight down from it.

setup.art: A thin beam starting 10 cm left of the middle line, hitting the middle of the mirror and bouncing back down to a pencil mark 10 cm right of the line, making a V.
setup.caption: 3. Aim at the middle of the mirror from the left. Mark where the bounce lands on the right.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: where the bounced beam landed
example_chart.x: Torch started this far left of the middle line
example_chart.y: Bounced beam landed this far right (cm)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be a little different.

flow.do: 1. Tape the slit card over the torch glass, or hold a comb in front of it. 2. Make the room dim by closing the curtains. 3. Lay the torch flat on the paper and switch it on.
flow.say: We need a thin beam of light, like a pencil line. Then we can see exactly where it goes.
flow.kid: Tape the card with the slit over your torch. Close the curtains. Lay the torch flat on the paper. Switch it on. See the thin line of light?
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the slit with scissors: about 2 mm wide and 3 cm long. A comb also works. It makes several thin beams.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bouncing-beam experiment. Here you make a thin beam of light so you can follow it.

flow.do: 1. Stand the mirror upright on the top edge of the paper, using plasticine or books. 2. Mark the middle of the mirror's bottom edge. 3. Draw a line with the ruler from that mark straight down to the bottom of the paper. 4. On the bottom edge, mark 5 cm, 10 cm and 15 cm to the left of the line.
flow.say: This middle line is our guide. We will start the torch on the left marks, and see where the light lands.
flow.kid: Stand the mirror up at the top of the paper. Draw a straight line down from its middle. Mark 5, 10 and 15 cm to the left of it.
flow.context: In the bouncing-beam experiment, a mirror stands at the top of a sheet of paper. Here you draw the guide line and the start marks.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess where the bounced beam will land if the torch starts at the 10 cm mark. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Before we try it, guess. If the torch starts 10 centimetres to the left, where will the light bounce to?
flow.kid: Guess first! If the torch starts 10 cm left, where will the light go?

check.q: The torch starts 10 cm to the left of the middle line. It aims at the middle of the mirror. Where will the bounced beam go?
options: It will spread all over the room
check.why: It goes to the right, because light leaves a mirror at the same slant it came in, on the other side. Picking 'straight back' usually means thinking a mirror always sends light back where it came from. That only happens when you shine straight at it. Picking 'all over the room' mixes a mirror up with a white wall, which scatters light. This is only a guess. Now test it.

flow.context: In the bouncing-beam experiment, a torch beam hits a mirror at a slant. Here you guess where the light will bounce.

flow.do: 1. Put the back of the torch on the 5 cm mark and aim its beam at the middle mark on the mirror. 2. Find where the bounced beam reaches the bottom edge. Make a mark there. 3. Measure how far right of the middle line it is. 4. Do the same from 10 cm and 15 cm. 5. Do each one twice.
flow.say: Let's test each start mark twice. Measure from the middle line to where the light lands.
flow.kid: Start at 5 cm. Aim at the middle of the mirror. Where does the light land? Mark it. Measure it. Now try 10 and 15.

ask.q: What do you notice about your numbers?
good: They match. 10 left goes to 10 right.
The further left I start, the further right it lands.

flow.parent: Expect the landing marks to be close to 5, 10 and 15 cm right of the line. If they are a few centimetres off, that is normal. The torch beam is a bit wide, and the mirror may not stand quite straight.
flow.context: In the bouncing-beam experiment, you start a torch at different marks on the left and aim at the middle of a mirror. Here you measure where each bounce lands.

flow.do: 1. With a ruler, draw each beam: a line from the start mark to the mirror, and a line from the mirror to the landing mark. 2. Fold the paper along the middle line.
flow.say: Each beam makes a V shape. Fold the paper on the middle line. Do the two sides of the V lie on top of each other?
flow.kid: Draw each beam as a V. Now fold the paper on the middle line. Do the two sides match?

check.q: When you fold the paper, the in-line and the out-line lie on top of each other. What does that show?
options: Light leaves the mirror at the same slant it came in
Light gets slower after it bounces
check.why: The two lines match because they have the same slant. The light came in at one slant and left at the same slant, on the other side. Scientists say the angle in equals the angle out. Picking 'the mirror made new light' usually means thinking a mirror is a light source. It is not. It only sends back the light that reaches it.

flow.context: In the bouncing-beam experiment, each beam makes a V on the paper. Here you fold the paper to compare the two sides of the V.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: light bounces off a mirror like a ball off a wall. What I saw: when the torch started 10 cm left, the light landed about 10 cm right, and the folded lines matched. Why: the mirror is smooth, so it sends the light off at the same slant it came in.
flow.think: Carrom players bounce the striker off the edge. Is that the same rule?
flow.context: This is the last step of the bouncing-beam experiment. You say what you found out, what showed it, and why.

experiments.fair_test: Use the same star shape each time, and the same mirror in the same place. Only the number of the try changes. Count every time the pencil goes outside the lines.
