materials.item: a mirror that stands up, or a mirror propped against books
3 copies of a star shape drawn with a double outline
a big book or a piece of card, to hide your hand
a pencil and a clock or phone timer

experiments.safety: Keep a glass mirror steady and in its frame.

schedule.what: Trace the star 3 times, looking only in the mirror. Time each try and count the slips.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each try, showing the number of slips.
experiments.context: In the mirror drawing race, you trace a star while you can only see your hand in a mirror. A mirror turns everything round from front to back, so your hand has to learn a new way.

setup.art: A star shape drawn with two outlines, one inside the other, on a sheet of paper, with a small mirror standing at the far edge of the paper.
setup.caption: 1. Put the star paper in front of a standing mirror.

setup.art: A child's hand holding a pencil on the star, hidden from the child's eyes by a big book held up like a wall, while the child looks only at the mirror.
setup.caption: 2. Hide your hand behind a book. Look only in the mirror.

setup.art: A pencil line wobbling between the two outlines of the star, with three small marks where it went outside.
setup.caption: 3. Trace between the lines. Count each time you slip out.

flow.do: 1. Draw a star with two outlines, about 1 cm apart. 2. Stand the mirror at the far side of the paper. 3. Hold a big book up so your child cannot see their hand directly, only in the mirror.
flow.say: You will trace this star in the gap between the lines. But you can only look in the mirror. Let's see how your hand copes.
flow.kid: Look only in the mirror. Trace the star between the two lines. Ready? Go!
flow.context: This is the first step of the mirror drawing race. You set up a star to trace while looking only in a mirror.

flow.do: 1. Time three tries. 2. After each try, count how many times the pencil went outside the lines. 3. Write both numbers in the table.
flow.say: Try it three times. I will time you, and we will count the slips.
flow.kid: Trace the star three times. Count your slips each time. Write them down.

ask.q: Which way was hard to move: away from you and towards you, or side to side?
good: Towards and away was hard, because the mirror turns that round.

flow.parent: Most people find moving towards and away from themselves hardest. That is the direction the mirror turns round. In 1962 the Canadian brain scientist Brenda Milner tested a famous patient with this star task. He got better each day, even though he could not remember practising. His hand learned without his memory.
flow.context: In the mirror drawing race, you trace a star looking only in a mirror. Here you time three tries and count your slips.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Did the slips go down from try 1 to try 3?
flow.say: Look at your numbers. Did your hand get better?
flow.kid: Look at your numbers. Did you slip less on try 3?

check.q: A child slipped 9 times on try 1, 6 times on try 2 and 3 times on try 3. What does that show?
options: Practice helped the hand learn the mirror's way
Mirrors only work after you use them a few times
check.why: The mirror and the star stayed the same. Only the child changed. Their hand and brain learned the mirror's front-to-back flip. Picking 'the mirror got smoother' usually means looking for the change in the wrong place. In a fair test, if only one thing changed, that is the cause.

flow.context: In the mirror drawing race, a child traces a star three times while looking only in a mirror, and counts the slips.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Like a scientist now. What do you think? What showed it? Why?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: it is hard to draw in a mirror, but you get better. What I saw: I slipped 8 times at first and 3 times on my last try. Why: the mirror turns front and back round, and my brain learned to turn it back.
flow.context: This is the last step of the mirror drawing race. You say what you think, what showed it, and why.

experiments.title: How Many of Me? Two mirrors and a toy
experiments.question: When two mirrors stand like an open book, how does the gap between them change the number of pictures?
experiments.predict: Guess: when you close the mirrors up to a smaller gap, will you see more pictures of the toy, fewer, or the same?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same toy in the same place, right in the middle between the mirrors. Change only the gap. Count each picture of the toy, but not the real toy.
results_table: Pictures of the toy I counted
Slices of the circle that fit in the gap

materials.item: 2 square mirrors or mirror tiles of the same size
strong tape, to join them like a book
a small toy, like a toy elephant or a coin
the printed gap guide: a circle cut into 2, 4, 6 and 8 equal slices

experiments.safety: A grown-up tapes the mirrors together, and covers any sharp edges with tape.

schedule.what: Tape two mirrors like a book. Stand them on the gap guide. Count the pictures of a toy at 4 gaps.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Look for a pattern between the slices and the pictures.
experiments.context: In this experiment you tape two mirrors together like a book and stand a toy between them. You count how many pictures of the toy you see as you close the gap.

example_chart.title: Pictures of one toy between two mirrors
example_chart.note: These are the numbers you should get if the mirrors stand exactly on the guide lines.

setup.art: Two square mirrors joined along one edge with tape, standing like a book opened halfway.
setup.caption: 1. Tape two mirrors along one edge, like a book.

setup.art: The joined mirrors standing on a paper circle divided into four slices, opened to fit exactly one quarter slice, with a toy elephant in the middle of the slice.
setup.caption: 2. Stand them on the gap guide. Put the toy in the middle.

setup.art: Looking into the two mirrors at a quarter gap, the toy elephant appears four times in a ring, the real one and three pictures.
setup.caption: 3. Count the pictures. Then close the gap and count again.

flow.do: 1. Put the two mirrors face down, side by side, touching. 2. Tape them along the edge where they touch, so they open and close like a book. 3. Stand them up, shiny sides facing in.
flow.say: We are making a mirror book. It will open and close.
flow.kid: Tape two mirrors together like a book. Stand them up. Shiny sides in.
flow.context: This is the first step of the two-mirrors experiment. Here a grown-up tapes two mirrors together like a book.

flow.do: 1. Stand the mirror book on the gap guide, opened to a quarter slice. 2. Put the toy in the middle of the slice. 3. Look in from the open side and count the pictures of the toy.
flow.say: How many elephants can you see? Count only the pictures, not the real one.
flow.kid: Open the mirrors to fit one quarter slice. Put your toy in the middle. Count the pictures. Don't count the real toy.
flow.parent: At a quarter gap you should count 3 pictures. Some children count the real toy too, and say 4. That is fine, as long as they say which they mean.
flow.context: In the two-mirrors experiment, two mirrors stand like an open book with a toy between them. Here you count the pictures at a quarter gap.

flow.do: 1. Close the mirrors to a sixth slice and count. 2. Then an eighth slice and count. 3. Then open them flat, to half the circle, and count. 4. Write each number in the table.
flow.say: Now let's make the gap smaller. What happens to the number of pictures?
flow.kid: Close the gap to a sixth slice. Count. Then an eighth. Count. Then open them flat. Count.

check.q: At a quarter gap you saw 3 pictures. At a sixth gap you saw 5. What will happen at an eighth gap?
check.why: Smaller gap means more pictures, because the light can bounce back and forth more times before it escapes. Picking 'fewer' usually means thinking a small gap squeezes the pictures out. Notice the pattern: the number of slices that fit in a whole circle, take away one. 8 slices, take away 1, is 7.

flow.context: In the two-mirrors experiment, you count pictures of a toy as you close the gap between two mirrors.

flow.do: Ask your child for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why does it happen?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a smaller gap makes more pictures. What I saw: a quarter gap made 3 pictures, and an eighth made 7. Why: light bounces from one mirror to the other and back. In a small gap it bounces more times, and every bounce makes a picture.
flow.think: A kaleidoscope has three mirrors in a narrow triangle. How many pictures might it make?
flow.context: This is the last step of the two-mirrors experiment. You say what you found, what showed it, and why.

activities.title: Spoon Faces and the Mirror Hunt

materials.item: a shiny steel spoon
5 things from around the home: a steel tumbler, a phone with its screen off, a bowl of water, a piece of foil, a wooden block

schedule.what: Spoon Faces and the Mirror Hunt

activities.record: Draw your face in the inside and the back of the spoon. List your 5 things under 'Shows a picture' or 'Only shines'.
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity. You look at your face in a spoon, then hunt for other things at home that show your face.

setup.art: A child looking at an upside-down reflection of their face in the hollow of a steel spoon.
setup.caption: 1. Look at your face in the inside of a spoon. Then the back.

setup.art: A tray holding a steel tumbler, a dark phone screen, a bowl of water, crumpled foil and a wooden block, with a child peering into the bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Hunt for 5 things. Which ones show your face?

flow.do: Give your child a steel spoon. Ask them to look into the hollow side, then the back.
flow.say: What do you notice about your face? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Look into the inside of the spoon. Now the back. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

good: It was upside down inside the spoon.
On the back it was the right way up but small.

flow.parent: Don't explain yet. Just collect what your child notices and wonders. The curved spoon bends the picture. We come back to flat mirrors next.
flow.context: This is the first step of a noticing activity. You look at your face in a steel spoon.

flow.do: 1. Put the 5 things on a tray. 2. Your child looks for their face in each one. 3. They sort them into two piles: 'Shows a picture' and 'Only shines'.
flow.say: Which of these show your face? Which only shine a bit, with no picture?
flow.kid: Look for your face in each thing. Make two piles. 'Shows a picture'. 'Only shines'.
flow.parent: Smooth things, like the tumbler, still water and the dark phone, show a picture. Crumpled foil only shines. The wooden block shows nothing. Ask why the smooth ones are different.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One last question about your piles.
flow.kid: Tap your answer.

check.q: Crumpled foil is shiny, but it shows no clear picture of your face. Why?
options: Its bumps send light off in all directions
Foil is too thin to reflect
check.why: Each tiny bump in crumpled foil faces a different way, so the light bounces off every which way and the picture gets mixed up. A smooth mirror sends all the light back in neat order. Picking 'foil makes its own light' mixes up shining with making light. Foil is not a light source. In a dark cupboard it does not shine at all.

activities.title: Mirror Twins

materials.item: a partner: a grown-up, brother, sister or friend

activities.safety: Clear a space so nobody bumps into furniture.
activities.record: Draw yourself and your mirror twin, each raising one hand. Colour the raised hands.
activities.context: Mirror Twins is a copying game. One person moves, and the other copies exactly, as if they were a mirror. It shows what a mirror really turns round.

setup.art: Two children facing each other, one raising a hand and the other copying like a reflection.
setup.caption: 1. Stand face to face, an arm's length apart.

setup.art: The leader slowly bends sideways and the mirror twin bends the same way, both leaning towards the same window.
setup.caption: 2. The leader moves slowly. The twin copies, like a mirror.

flow.do: 1. Stand face to face. 2. One person leads with slow moves: lifting a hand, tilting the head, touching an ear. 3. The other copies, like a mirror. 4. Swap after one minute.
flow.say: You are my mirror. Whatever I do, you do, at the same time. Go slowly, so the mirror can keep up.
flow.kid: Face your partner. They move slowly. You copy, like a mirror. Then swap.
flow.parent: This is from the founder's notes: children love the mimic game. Keep it slow and silent. Then ask the question in the next step.
flow.context: This is the first step of Mirror Twins, a copying game where one person acts as the other's mirror.

flow.do: Raise your right hand. Watch which hand the mirror twin raises.
flow.say: I raised my right hand. Which hand did you raise? Is it on the same side of the room as mine?
flow.kid: Your partner raises their right hand. You copy, like a mirror. Which hand did you raise? Is it on the same side of the room?

check.q: You face your partner and copy their raised right hand, like a mirror. Which of your hands goes up?
options: My left hand, on the same side of the room as theirs
My right hand, on the other side of the room
Neither, because mirrors swap up and down
check.why: A mirror keeps everything on the same side of the room. So to copy like a mirror, you raise the hand on their side, which is your left. What the mirror turns round is front and back: you face each other. Picking 'my right hand' is how a friend would copy, not a mirror. That is why we feel mirrors swap left and right.

flow.think: Does a mirror swap left and right, or front and back?

activities.title: Secret Mirror Messages

materials.item: paper and a dark felt pen
a hand mirror

activities.record: Write a secret message in mirror writing. Stick it on the fridge for your family to read with a mirror.
activities.context: In this activity you learn to write in mirror writing. Mirror writing runs backwards, so it reads properly in a mirror. Ambulances use it.

setup.art: A child holding a hand mirror upright beside a card with backwards letters, the letters reading the right way in the mirror.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a mirror upright next to your writing.

setup.art: A child writing their name backwards, checking each letter in a mirror propped at the end of the line.
setup.caption: 2. Write a word backwards. Check it in the mirror.

flow.do: 1. Write your child's name in big letters. 2. Stand the mirror upright at the end of the word. 3. Look at the word in the mirror.
flow.say: Look at your name in the mirror. What happened to it?
flow.kid: Write your name big. Hold the mirror at the end of it. What do you see?

good: It reads from right to left.

flow.context: This is the first step of Secret Mirror Messages. You look at normal writing in a mirror to see what happens to it.

flow.do: 1. Now your child writes their name backwards, so it reads properly in the mirror. 2. They start at the right edge and write one letter at a time, turning each letter round. 3. They check in the mirror after each letter.
flow.say: Now the other way. Write it so the mirror turns it the right way round. Start at the right side of the paper.
flow.kid: Write your name backwards. Start on the right. Turn each letter round. Check in the mirror.
flow.parent: Some children find this easy, especially left-handers. Others need many tries. Both are normal. Leonardo da Vinci, the great Italian artist, wrote his notebooks this way about 500 years ago. Nobody knows for sure why.
flow.context: In Secret Mirror Messages, you write words backwards so a mirror turns them the right way round.

flow.do: Show a picture of an ambulance, or look out for one. Point at the backwards word on its front.
flow.say: Why do you think AMBULANCE is written backwards on the front?
flow.kid: Look at the front of an ambulance. The word is backwards! Why?

check.q: Why is AMBULANCE written backwards on the front of an ambulance?
options: So drivers in front can read it in their mirrors
Because the painter made a mistake
So only the ambulance driver can read it
check.why: Drivers in front see the ambulance in their rear-view mirror. The mirror turns writing round. So the word is painted backwards, and the mirror turns it the right way. Then the driver reads AMBULANCE and moves aside. Picking 'a mistake' is a fair first guess, but every ambulance has it, so it must be on purpose.

flow.context: In Secret Mirror Messages, you learn about mirror writing. Here you look at why ambulances have backwards writing.

flow.do: Your child writes one short secret message in mirror writing for the family.
flow.say: Write a secret message for the family. Only someone with a mirror can read it!
flow.kid: Write a short secret message backwards. Stick it on the fridge. Who can read it?

activities.title: Half a Picture: finish it with a mirror

materials.item: the printed half-pictures: half a butterfly, half a face, half a leaf, half a house, half a letter A
a hand mirror
a pencil

schedule.what: Half a Picture: finish it with a mirror

activities.record: Draw the missing half of each picture. Then list the capital letters that look the same in a mirror.
activities.context: In this activity you use a mirror to finish half-pictures. The mirror shows the missing half. This is called symmetry.

setup.art: Half a butterfly drawn on paper, with a small mirror standing upright on the straight edge, making a whole butterfly appear.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the mirror on the straight edge of the half-picture.

setup.art: A child drawing the missing half of a leaf, copying what they saw in the mirror.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the missing half. Check it with the mirror.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the half-pictures. 2. Stand the mirror on the straight edge of the half butterfly. 3. Look into the mirror from the drawing's side.
flow.say: Look, a whole butterfly! The mirror made the other half. Shapes whose two halves match like this have symmetry.
flow.kid: Stand the mirror on the straight edge. Look! A whole butterfly. Try the other half-pictures.
flow.context: This is the first step of the half-picture activity. A mirror on the edge of half a picture makes it look whole.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws the missing half of each picture. 2. They check it with the mirror.
flow.say: Now draw the missing half yourself. Then check with the mirror. Does it match?
flow.kid: Draw the missing half. Check with your mirror. Does it match?
flow.parent: This links to maths: line symmetry. The edge where the mirror stands is called the line of symmetry.

flow.do: Write the capital letters A to Z. Your child stands the mirror down the middle of each letter.
flow.say: Which letters look the same in a mirror? Put the mirror down the middle of each one.
flow.kid: Write A to Z in capitals. Stand the mirror down the middle of each. Which ones stay the same?

check.q: Which of these words looks the same when you stand a mirror next to it?
check.why: M and O look the same in a mirror stood beside them, and MOM reads the same both ways, so the mirror shows MOM. D, B and S turn round in a mirror, so DAD, BOB and SIS look wrong. Picking DAD or BOB usually means only checking that the word reads the same backwards. The letters must also be symmetrical.

flow.parent: Letters that look the same in a mirror stood beside them: A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y.

activities.title: The Sunlight Postman

materials.item: a small mirror, plastic if possible
paper targets stuck on a shady wall
a sunny window or courtyard

activities.safety: A grown-up must be there. Never look at the Sun. Never bounce sunlight into anyone's eyes, or at animals, cars or the road. Bounced sunlight is bright enough to hurt eyes.
activities.record: Draw where you stood, where the Sun was and where the bright spot landed. Draw the light's path as two straight lines.
activities.context: The Sunlight Postman is an outdoor activity. You catch sunlight with a mirror and send a bright spot onto targets on a shady wall, like delivering light.

setup.art: A child standing in a sunny spot holding a small mirror, with a bright patch of light landing on a paper target on a shady wall.
setup.caption: 1. Stand in the sun. Catch sunlight on the mirror.

setup.art: A dark corner of a room lit up by a bright spot of sunlight bounced in from a mirror at the window.
setup.caption: 2. Post light into a dark corner.

flow.do: 1. Stick 3 paper targets on a shady wall, at different heights. 2. Stand in the sun with your child. 3. Tilt the mirror until a bright spot appears on the wall.
flow.say: The mirror catches sunlight and sends it on, like a postman. Can you deliver the spot to the first target?
flow.kid: Stand in the sun with a grown-up. Tilt your mirror. Find the bright spot on the wall. Can you move it to a target?
flow.parent: Watch that the spot never goes near anyone's face. The spot moves twice as fast as the mirror turns, so small tilts are best.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sunlight Postman. You use a mirror to bounce a bright spot of sunlight onto targets on a wall.

flow.do: 1. Try to hit each target. 2. Then go inside and bounce sunlight from a window into the darkest corner of a room.
flow.say: Can you post light into the darkest corner? People did this in palaces long ago, with walls full of mirrors.
flow.kid: Hit each target. Then bounce sunlight into a dark corner indoors.
flow.parent: The Sheesh Mahal, the palace of mirrors at Amber Fort near Jaipur, is covered in tiny mirrors. People say a few lamps make the whole hall sparkle.

flow.do: Ask the check question, then claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Why does the spot move when you tilt the mirror? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Tap your answer. Then say: what I think, what I saw, why.

check.q: You tilt the mirror a little, and the bright spot on the wall jumps across. Why?
options: The light leaves at a new slant, so it lands in a new place
check.why: When you tilt the mirror, the light hits it at a new slant, so it leaves at a new slant too. A small tilt makes a big jump on a faraway wall. Picking 'the Sun moved' is a fair idea, because the Sun does move slowly across the sky. But it cannot jump in one second.

activities.title: How Big a Mirror Do You Need?

materials.item: a bathroom or wall mirror
2 small sticky notes or bindis

schedule.what: How Big a Mirror Do You Need?

activities.record: Measure your face, and the gap between the two notes. Write both numbers.
activities.context: In this activity you mark the top of your head and your chin on a mirror. You find out how much mirror you really need to see your whole face.

setup.art: A child at a bathroom mirror putting a sticky note where the top of their head appears, and another where their chin appears.
setup.caption: 1. Stick a note at the top of your head in the mirror, and one at your chin.

setup.art: The same child two steps back from the mirror, their reflected face still fitting exactly between the two sticky notes.
setup.caption: 2. Step back. Does your face still fit between the notes?

flow.do: 1. Your child stands close to the mirror. 2. You stick a note where the top of their head appears in the mirror, and one where their chin appears, as they tell you. 3. Measure the gap between the notes. 4. Measure their real face from head to chin.
flow.say: Let's mark where your face is in the mirror. Then we'll measure the gap.
flow.kid: Stand close to the mirror. Tell your grown-up where to stick the notes. One at your head, one at your chin. Measure the gap. Now measure your real face.
flow.parent: The gap on the mirror is about half your child's real face. A 20 cm face fits in about 10 cm of mirror.
flow.context: This is the first step of the mirror-size activity. You mark the top of your head and your chin on a mirror and measure.

flow.do: 1. Your child takes two big steps back. 2. Does their face still fit between the notes? 3. Try four steps back.
flow.say: Step back. Did your face shrink out of the notes, or stay between them?
flow.kid: Take two big steps back. Is your face still between the notes? Try four steps.

check.q: You step back from the mirror. Your face in the mirror still fits between the same two notes. What does that show?
options: The mirror space you need does not change when you step back
You need a bigger mirror when you are further away
check.why: The picture of your face looks smaller as you step back, but the patch of mirror it uses stays the same. You always need a mirror half as tall as you to see all of you. Picking 'you need a bigger mirror' is what most grown-ups guess. Your test shows it is not true.

flow.parent: This surprises most grown-ups. To see your whole body, you need a mirror only half your height, at any distance.

flow.do: Ask: how tall a mirror would you need to see your whole body?
flow.say: You are about how tall? So how tall a mirror would you need?
flow.kid: How tall are you? Halve it. That is the mirror you need to see all of you!

activities.title: The Endless Corridor

materials.item: 2 hand mirrors, or a hand mirror and a wall mirror
a small toy or a lit torch

activities.safety: Hold glass mirrors by their frames.
activities.record: Write the biggest number of pictures you could count. Draw how the far ones looked.
activities.context: In the Endless Corridor you hold two mirrors face to face and look at the pictures going on and on. It comes from the founder's Zero and Infinity game.

setup.art: A child holding a hand mirror facing a wall mirror, with a long tunnel of smaller and smaller copies of the mirror stretching away.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a hand mirror facing a big mirror. Peek over the top.

setup.art: A close view of the tunnel, the far copies getting darker and greener.
setup.caption: 2. Count the copies. Look at the far ones closely.

flow.do: 1. Hold a hand mirror facing the wall mirror, a little apart. 2. Put a small toy or a lit torch between them. 3. Your child peeks over the edge and counts the copies.
flow.say: Count the pictures. Keep going as far as you can. The longer you count, the better!
flow.kid: Hold a mirror facing the big mirror. Peek over the top. Count the pictures. How far can you go?
flow.parent: This is the founder's 'infinite reflections' game. Make it a race: who can count the most?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Endless Corridor. You hold two mirrors face to face and count the pictures.

flow.do: Look closely at the farthest pictures.
flow.say: Are the far pictures as bright as the near ones? What colour are they?
flow.kid: Look at the far pictures. Are they bright or dark? Do they look a bit green?

check.q: In two facing mirrors, the far pictures get darker and then disappear. Why?
options: Each bounce loses a little light
The mirrors run out of glass
check.why: Every time light bounces, the mirror keeps a little of it. After many bounces, so little light is left that the pictures fade. The glass also soaks up a little red light, so the far pictures look greenish. Picking 'light gets tired' is close in spirit. Light does not slow down, but it does lose a bit at each bounce.

flow.think: If a mirror lost no light at all, would the corridor really go on for ever?

activities.title: Mirror Mirror on the Wall: draw how you feel

materials.item: a paper plate covered in foil, or a hand mirror
a large sheet of paper and crayons

schedule.what: Mirror Mirror on the Wall: draw how you feel

activities.record: Keep the drawing. Write one line under it: 'This is me, inside.'
activities.context: In this art activity you look at your face in a mirror, then draw yourself as you feel inside. It is from the founder's activity list.

setup.art: A child gazing quietly into a mirror on a table, crayons beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Look at your face in the mirror for one quiet minute.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a mirror frame with a self-portrait inside, full of colours and small pictures of things they love.
setup.caption: 2. Draw yourself inside a mirror frame, as you feel.

flow.do: Your child looks at their face in the mirror for one quiet minute.
flow.say: Look at your face for one minute. Just look. You have never seen your own face without a mirror or a photo.
flow.kid: Look at your face in the mirror. Just look, for one minute. Your face is light, bouncing back to you.
flow.context: This is the first step of an art activity. You look quietly at your face in a mirror before you draw.

flow.do: 1. Draw a big mirror frame on the paper. 2. Inside it, your child draws themselves the way they feel inside, not only how they look.
flow.say: The mirror shows the outside of you. Now draw what the mirror cannot show: how you feel, what you love, what you dream about.
flow.kid: Draw a big mirror frame. Inside it, draw you. Not only your face. Draw how you feel inside.
flow.parent: There is no right answer. Ask: what does your drawing show that the real mirror can't?
flow.think: What does a mirror show about you? What can it never show?

activities.title: Be the Light: act out a bounce

materials.item: a soft ball
a wall, and a strip of tape on the floor

activities.safety: Use a soft ball, away from windows.

schedule.what: Be the Light: act out a bounce

activities.record: Draw the path of the ball, and the path of a child acting as light, as V shapes.
activities.context: In this act-it-out activity, children pretend to be light and bounce off a wall like a mirror. It comes from the founder's idea of miming light bouncing between mirrors.

setup.art: A child rolling a soft ball at a slant towards a wall, and the ball bouncing away at the same slant.
setup.caption: 1. Roll a ball at a slant to the wall. Watch where it goes.

setup.art: A child walking at a slant towards a wall, touching it with both hands, then walking away at the same slant like light.
setup.caption: 2. Now you are the light. Walk in, bounce, walk out at the same slant.

flow.do: 1. Stick a strip of tape on the floor, straight out from the wall. 2. Roll the ball at a slant so it hits the wall where the tape meets it. 3. Watch where it rolls away.
flow.say: Light bounces like this ball. It comes in at a slant and leaves at the same slant.
flow.kid: Roll the ball at a slant. Hit the wall where the tape is. Where does it go?
flow.context: This is the first step of Be the Light. You roll a ball at a wall to see how things bounce.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks at a slant to the tape mark, touches the wall and walks away at the same slant. 2. Another family member acts as an eye, and stands where the light should go.
flow.say: You are a beam of light! Walk in at a slant. Bounce off the mirror wall. Walk out at the same slant, straight to the eye.
flow.kid: You are light! Walk in at a slant. Touch the wall. Walk out at the same slant. Can you reach the person being the eye?

check.q: A light beam hits a mirror coming in steeply. How does it leave?
options: Just as steeply, on the other side
Straight back the way it came
check.why: Light always leaves a flat mirror at the same slant it came in. Steep in means steep out. Picking 'straight back' only happens when light hits the mirror head on. Picking 'it stops' mixes a mirror up with a black cloth, which soaks up light.

projects.title: Make a Kaleidoscope

materials.item: a sheet of mirror card or thin plastic mirror sheet, about the size of a notebook
a cardboard tube, like a kitchen-roll tube
tape, a ruler and scissors
a small handful of beads, sequins or bits of coloured paper
cling film and a clear plastic lid, or tracing paper
paint or stickers to decorate

projects.safety: Use mirror card or plastic mirror sheet, never glass. A grown-up cuts the strips. Small beads are a choking risk for babies, so keep them away from little brothers and sisters.

schedule.what: Cut three mirror strips. Tape them into a triangle tube. Slide it into the cardboard tube.
Make the bead end. Decorate the tube. Look, turn and draw the patterns.

projects.record: Draw three patterns you saw. Count the copies of one bead in a pattern. Write how many there were.
projects.context: In this 2-day project you make a kaleidoscope: a tube with three mirrors inside. The mirrors make many copies of a few beads, so you see a pattern like a flower.

setup.art: Three strips of mirror card taped into a long triangle tube with the shiny sides facing in.
setup.caption: 1. Tape three mirror strips into a triangle tube, shiny sides in.

setup.art: The mirror triangle sliding into a kitchen-roll tube, with a cap of cling film holding a few coloured beads at one end.
setup.caption: 2. Slide it into a cardboard tube. Add a bead cap at one end.

setup.art: The view inside a homemade kaleidoscope: a six-sided flower of coloured beads.
setup.caption: 3. Look through the open end and turn the tube.

flow.do: 1. Measure three strips of mirror card, each as long as the tube and about 3 cm wide. 2. A grown-up cuts them. 3. Lay them side by side, shiny side down, with a tiny gap between them. 4. Tape across them.
flow.say: We are making a triangle of mirrors. Light from the beads will bounce between them again and again.
flow.kid: Measure three strips as long as your tube. A grown-up cuts them. Lay them shiny side down. Tape across them.
flow.context: This is the first step of making a kaleidoscope, a tube with three mirrors inside. Here you cut and tape the mirror strips.

flow.do: 1. Fold the taped strips into a triangle tube, shiny sides in. 2. Tape the last edge. 3. Slide the triangle into the cardboard tube.
flow.say: Look down the triangle. What do you see already?
flow.kid: Fold the strips into a triangle. Shiny sides in. Tape it. Slide it into the tube. Peek in!
flow.wait: Leave the tube overnight so the tape sets. Day 2 makes the bead end.

flow.do: 1. Stretch cling film over one end and push it in a little to make a cup. 2. Drop in the beads. 3. Cover with a clear lid or tracing paper and tape it on.
flow.say: These few beads will turn into a whole flower.
flow.kid: Make a cling film cup at one end. Drop in a few beads. Cover it and tape it.

check.q: There are only 6 beads in your kaleidoscope, but you see a flower made of many. Where do the extra beads come from?
options: The mirrors make copies of the light from the beads
check.why: Light from the beads bounces from mirror to mirror. Each bounce makes another picture of the beads. So a few real beads make a whole flower of pictures. Picking 'the beads break' usually means thinking each picture must be a real thing. Like your image in a mirror, the pictures are made only of light.

flow.do: 1. Your child looks through the open end towards a window, and slowly turns the tube. 2. They draw three patterns. 3. They count the copies of one bead.
flow.say: Turn it slowly. Every turn makes a new pattern. Can a pattern ever come back exactly the same?
flow.kid: Look towards the window. Turn the tube slowly. Draw three patterns. Count the copies of one bead.
flow.parent: The kaleidoscope was invented by the Scottish scientist David Brewster in 1816. He named it from Greek words meaning 'looking at beautiful shapes'. With three mirrors you usually see the same bead about 6 times in the middle flower.
flow.think: If you shake the beads, will the same pattern ever come back?

challenges.title: Light the Hidden Toy
challenges.problem: A toy is hiding behind a box. A torch is fixed in one place and cannot be moved. Your job is to light up the toy using mirrors.
constraints: You cannot move the torch or the box.
The light must not touch anyone's eyes.
Use as few mirrors as you can.
materials: a torch on a pile of books
2 or 3 small mirrors and some plasticine to stand them up
general: Put one mirror where the torch beam hits, and tilt it to send the light round the side of the box.
If one bounce is not enough, add a second mirror past the corner of the box.
Draw the path first, as straight lines with a corner at each mirror.
creative: Use the shiny side of a steel plate or a piece of smooth foil as an extra mirror.
Bounce the light off the ceiling, if your ceiling is white. It will be dim, but it may reach.
Two mirrors at the right angle can send light back exactly the way it came. Bicycle reflectors work like this.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw the path of the light, try it, and count the mirrors. Can you do it with fewer?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A toy hides behind a box, and a torch cannot be moved. You must steer the light round the box using mirrors.

setup.art: A torch on books shining at a cardboard box, with a small toy hidden in the shadow behind the box.
setup.caption: 1. The torch shines on the box. The toy is in the dark.

setup.art: A small mirror on plasticine beside the box, sending the torch beam round the corner onto the toy.
setup.caption: 2. Place a mirror to send the light round the box.

flow.do: 1. Set up the torch, box and toy. 2. Ask your child to draw a plan of where the light must go.
flow.say: Light travels in straight lines. So how can we make it go round a corner?
flow.kid: Look at the box and the toy. Draw a plan. Where must the light go?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Light the Hidden Toy challenge. You plan how to steer torchlight round a box using mirrors.

flow.do: Your child places mirrors, tests, and changes them until the toy is lit.
flow.say: Try it. If the spot misses, tilt the mirror a tiny bit.
flow.kid: Put a mirror in the beam. Tilt it. Can you light the toy? Add another mirror if you need to.

check.q: Your mirror sends the light past the toy, too far to the right. What will fix it?
options: Tilt the mirror a little to change the slant
Wait for the light to come back
check.why: The light leaves at the same slant it arrives. Tilt the mirror, and the slant changes, so the spot moves. Picking 'move the toy' breaks the rules of the challenge. Engineers must solve the problem as it is.

flow.do: Try the creative ideas, then your child's own idea.
flow.say: Can you do it with fewer mirrors, or with something that is not a mirror at all?
flow.kid: Try a steel plate or smooth foil. Can you do it a new way?

flow.do: Your child explains their best design, using the words slant and bounce.
flow.say: Tell me how your light got to the toy.
flow.kid: Explain your best design. Use the words bounce and slant.

challenges.title: See the Back of Your Own Head
challenges.problem: You have never seen the back of your own head. Find a way to see it, using mirrors.
constraints: You may not use a phone camera.
Use only mirrors you have at home.
general: Stand with your back to the wall mirror. Hold the hand mirror in front of your face. Tilt it until you see the wall mirror in it.
The light bounces twice: off the back of your head to the wall mirror, then to the hand mirror, then to your eyes.
creative: Tailors' shops have three mirrors in a fold, so you can see your back and sides at once.
Try a steel tumbler as the second mirror. How clear is the picture?
With two mirrors, writing comes out the right way round again. Hold up a word and see.
challenges.your_turn: Can you see your own left ear? Your own feet from behind? Invent a way, and draw the path of the light.
challenges.context: This is a puzzle challenge. You use two mirrors to see the back of your own head, which you have never seen directly.

setup.art: A child standing with their back to a bathroom mirror, holding a hand mirror in front of their face and seeing the back of their head in it.
setup.caption: 1. Back to the big mirror. Hand mirror in front of your face.

setup.art: A diagram of light bouncing from the back of a child's head to a wall mirror, then to a hand mirror, then into the child's eyes.

flow.do: Your child stands with their back to the wall mirror and tries the hand mirror.
flow.say: Can you see the back of your head? How many bounces does the light make?
flow.kid: Stand with your back to the big mirror. Hold the small mirror in front. Tilt it. Can you see the back of your head?
flow.context: This is the first step of the challenge to see the back of your own head with two mirrors.

flow.do: Hold up a word on paper and look at it through both mirrors.
flow.say: With two mirrors, does the writing look backwards?
flow.kid: Hold up a word behind your head. Look in the small mirror. Is it backwards?

check.q: You look at a word through two mirrors, one bounce after another. How does the word look?
check.why: The first mirror turns the word round. The second mirror turns it round again. Two turns put it back the right way. Picking 'backwards' is right for one mirror. The trick is to count the bounces.

flow.do: Your child draws the path of the light.
flow.say: Draw where the light went, from your head to your eyes.
flow.kid: Draw the light's path. Put an arrow on each straight line.

quiz.why: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. Picking 'made by a mirror' means thinking a mirror is a light source. It is not.

quiz.p: Is a mirror a light source?
quiz.why: A mirror makes no light. In a dark cupboard it shows nothing. Picking 'only in the daytime' is close: it needs light from somewhere, but the light is not its own.

quiz.p: A torch shines at a mirror from the left, at a slant. Where does the light go?
opts: Off to the right, at the same slant
quiz.why: Light leaves a mirror at the same slant it came in, on the other side. Picking 'straight back' only happens when you shine head on.

quiz.p: When you fold the bouncing-beam paper on the middle line, the in-line and out-line match. What does this show?
opts: The angle in equals the angle out
quiz.why: Matching lines have the same slant. That is the rule for mirrors. Picking 'light bends in the air' mixes reflection up with a different idea.

quiz.p: Why does a white wall show no picture of you?
opts: Its tiny bumps scatter the light every way
quiz.why: A white wall reflects lots of light, but scatters it. Picking 'reflects no light' is very common. If it reflected none, it would look black.

quiz.p: Why is AMBULANCE written backwards on the front of an ambulance?
opts: A mirror turns it round so drivers in front can read it
So the patient can read it
quiz.why: Drivers see the ambulance in their rear-view mirror, and the mirror turns the writing round the right way.

quiz.p: What does a mirror really turn round?
quiz.why: Your image faces you, so front and back are turned round. Up stays up, and your raised hand stays on the same side of the room. Picking 'up and down' comes from spoons, which are curved.

quiz.p: Two mirrors stand like an open book at a quarter gap. How many pictures of a toy do you see?
quiz.why: 4 slices fit in a circle. Take away 1 for the real toy. That leaves 3 pictures. Picking 4 means counting the real toy too.

quiz.p: Which letter stays the same when you stand a mirror beside it?
quiz.why: H has a line of symmetry straight down its middle. R, S and N turn round.

quiz.p: How do scientists measure the distance to the Moon with mirrors?
opts: They bounce laser light off mirrors left there and time it
They use a very long tape
They look at the Moon in a bathroom mirror
quiz.why: Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon in 1969. Scientists time how long a laser pulse takes to bounce back.

quiz.p: Why do big telescopes use curved mirrors?
opts: To gather faint starlight into one bright picture
quiz.why: A curved mirror gathers lots of faint light into one small spot, so we can see very faraway stars.

quiz.p: Do scientists agree about what the mirror test shows?
opts: No. They still argue, for example about a fish that passed it
quiz.why: Apes, elephants and magpies pass. In 2019 a small fish did too. Scientists still argue about what passing really means.

quiz.p: Why do far pictures fade in two facing mirrors?
opts: Each bounce loses a little light
The mirror runs out of pictures
quiz.why: No mirror is perfect. A little light is lost every time it bounces.

applications: Car, bus and scooter mirrors let drivers see what is behind them.
Ambulances and fire engines write their names backwards on the front, so drivers read them in their mirrors.
Mirrors on hill-road bends in the ghats let drivers see round corners.
Dentists use a tiny mirror on a stick to see the backs of your teeth.
Torches, car headlights and lighthouses use curved mirrors to send light forward in a strong beam.
Big telescopes, like the James Webb Space Telescope, use mirrors to gather faint starlight.
Scientists bounce lasers off mirrors left on the Moon to measure its distance.
Bicycle reflectors and the cat's eyes on highways send headlight beams straight back to drivers.
Solar kitchens use rows of curved mirrors to bounce sunlight onto one spot and make steam for cooking. A famous temple kitchen in Shirdi, Maharashtra, does this.
Long ago, armies sent messages over many kilometres by flashing sunlight with mirrors.
Kaleidoscopes, mirror mazes and mirror-work embroidery use mirrors to make beautiful patterns.
Shops and small flats use wall mirrors to look bigger and brighter.
Barbers and tailors use two or three mirrors so you can see the back of your head.

open_questions.q: Why do only some animals seem to know their own face in a mirror?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists disagree about what the mirror test measures. A small fish passing it in 2019 made the argument bigger.

open_questions.q: Why did Leonardo da Vinci write in mirror writing?
open_questions.why_open: He never explained. Some think it was so he did not smudge the ink, and some think it kept his notes private. Nobody knows.

open_questions.q: Why does life use only one of the two mirror forms of many molecules?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several ideas, from pure luck to something in space tipping the balance. None has been proved.

open_questions.q: Is there a deep reason why one of nature's forces behaves differently in a mirror world?
open_questions.why_open: Chien-Shiung Wu showed in 1957 that the weak force does. Physicists still do not know why nature is built that way.
Mirrors keep getting better, but every real mirror loses a little light. Scientists think a perfect one may be impossible.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does the brain know that the face in the mirror is me?
open_questions.why_open: Babies learn it at about 18 months. Scientists are still finding out what happens in the brain when they do.

open_questions.q: Did Archimedes really burn ships with mirrors?
open_questions.why_open: The story was written down hundreds of years later. Tests have given mixed results, and historians still argue.

maths.problem: In the bouncing-beam test, Riya started the torch 5 cm, 10 cm and 15 cm to the left of the middle line. Her bounced beams landed 5 cm, 10 cm and 14 cm to the right. Which one did not match exactly, and by how much?
maths.answer: The 15 cm one. It landed at 14 cm, which is 1 cm short.
maths.explain: 5 matches 5. 10 matches 10. 15 and 14 do not match. 15 take away 14 is 1. So it was 1 cm short. A small gap like this happens when the beam is a bit wide or the mirror leans.
maths.context: This is about the bouncing-beam test. You aim a thin torch beam at a mirror from marks on the left, and measure where the bounce lands on the right.
maths.why_maths: Taking away tells us how close a result came to what the rule says. A small difference means the rule held, and our test was a little bumpy.

maths.problem: Two mirrors make 3 pictures at a quarter gap, 5 at a sixth gap and 7 at an eighth gap. How many pictures will they make at a tenth gap?
maths.explain: Look at the pattern. 4 slices gives 3. 6 slices gives 5. 8 slices gives 7. Each time, the pictures are one less than the slices. 10 slices take away 1 is 9.
maths.context: This is about the two-mirrors experiment. You tape two mirrors like a book, put a toy between them, and count the pictures as you close the gap.

chart.title: Pictures of one toy between two mirrors
chart.x: Slices that fit in a circle

maths.why_maths: Finding a number pattern lets you predict a result before you test it. Then the test checks your prediction.

maths.problem: Arjun is 120 cm tall. To see his whole body in a mirror, he needs a mirror half his height. How tall must the mirror be?
maths.explain: Half of 120 is 60. You can check: 60 + 60 = 120. So a 60 cm mirror, hung at the right height, shows all of Arjun, wherever he stands.
maths.context: This is about the mirror-size activity. You stick notes on a mirror at the top of your head and your chin, and find the mirror only needs to be half as tall as your face.
maths.why_maths: Halving turns what we found with the sticky notes into a rule we can use, for example when buying a mirror for a bedroom wall.

maths.problem: In the mirror drawing race, Meera slipped outside the lines 9 times on try 1, 6 times on try 2 and 3 times on try 3. By how many slips did she get better each time?
maths.explain: 9 take away 6 is 3. 6 take away 3 is 3. So she slipped 3 fewer times on each new try.
maths.context: This is about the mirror drawing race. You trace a star while looking only in a mirror, three times, and count how often the pencil slips out of the lines.

chart.title: Meera's slips in the mirror drawing race

maths.why_maths: Finding the difference between tries shows how fast your brain is learning the mirror's way.

maths.problem: Draw a line of symmetry on each of these capital letters: A, H, M, T. Which one has two lines of symmetry?
maths.answer: H has two: one straight down the middle and one straight across.
maths.explain: Stand a mirror down the middle of each letter. All four look the same. Now lay the mirror across the middle. Only H still looks the same. So H has two lines of symmetry.
maths.context: This is about the half-picture activity and the Mirror or Not? game. You stand a mirror on letters and pictures to see which ones look the same in a mirror.
maths.why_maths: A line of symmetry is exactly where a mirror can stand and show the same shape. Symmetry is the maths of mirrors.

roots.context: We have been learning how mirrors send light back. Now we ask what mirrors tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: You have never seen your own face. You know it only from light the world sends back to you.
deep_truth.habit: We think we know ourselves from the inside, all by ourselves. But even our own face reaches us only by bouncing off something else: a mirror, water, a photo, a friend's eyes. Knowing yourself happens in a meeting with the world, not alone.
deep_truth.evidence: Without a mirror or water, you cannot see your own face at all. Babies only learn the face in the mirror is them at about 18 months.

three.who_am_i: Your face in the mirror is your own light, coming back to you. You are known through what you give out.
three.what_is_life: Living things carry mirrors too: a cat's eye, a fish's scales, a scallop's tiny eyes. Life uses light that bounces back.
three.what_is_this_world: Almost everything you see is reflected light. The world is always passing light back and forth.

roots.thread: One Sun sends out light. That light bounces off the Moon, the sea, a leaf, your face and a mirror, and becomes millions of different pictures. Two mirrors facing each other turn one toy into a whole crowd. DeepKids believes this is the One showing up as the many. The light is the same light, only bounced and shared. Each of us is like a mirror, showing the same light in our own way.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: Picture a huge net with a shining jewel at every knot. Each jewel reflects every other jewel, and every reflection holds all the others too, on and on.
teachings.link: Two facing mirrors do the same. Each mirror holds a picture of the other, which holds a picture of the first, again and again.

teachings.teaching: The wise person uses their mind like a mirror. It does not chase things or hold on to them. It shows whatever comes, and keeps nothing.
teachings.link: A mirror shows whatever stands in front of it, then lets it go. It does not store the picture after you walk away.

teachings.source: The Platform Sutra of Huineng, chapter 1
teachings.teaching: One monk wrote that the mind is like a mirror that must be wiped clean every day. Huineng, a kitchen worker who could not read, answered that the bright mirror was clean all along. There was nowhere for dust to land.
teachings.link: A mirror is useful only when it is smooth and clear. These teachers asked: is our mind clear already, or must we polish it?

science.text: Every mirror image is light passed on by trillions of electrons in the mirror's metal. They catch the light and send it back out.
Only a few kinds of animals seem to know their own face in a mirror. Scientists still argue about what this tells us about having a sense of self.

other_view.view: Knowing yourself in a mirror is a skill the brain learns, step by step, around 18 months old. It is a clever brain trick. They see no need for a deeper One behind it, and that is an honest view.

practice.title: The quiet mirror
practice.say: Let's sit in front of a mirror together. Look at your eyes in the mirror for a slow count of ten. Breathe in and out slowly. Now smile. Watch the mirror smile back. Close your eyes. Can you still feel your face, without seeing it? Open them. Which is you: the one feeling, or the one in the glass?
practice.kid: Sit in front of a mirror. Look at your eyes. Breathe slowly for ten counts. Smile, and watch it smile back. Close your eyes. Can you still feel your face?

ask: Is the face in the mirror you, or only your light?
If nobody and nothing ever reflected you, would you still know who you are?
When you smile at someone and they smile back, are they a bit like a mirror?
